a: Songs can instantly change our mood or trigger strong memories because of the unique way music is processed in the brain. Music activates multiple brain regions simultaneously, including the auditory cortex, limbic system (which processes emotions), and the hippocampus (which forms and retrieves memories). The limbic system has direct connections to the autonomic nervous system, which is why music can instantly trigger emotional responses like chills, tears, or euphoria. Music-evoked autobiographical memories (MEAMs) are particularly powerful because the olfactory and auditory pathways to memory are more direct than other sensory pathways. When a song is paired with a significant life event — a first dance, a concert, a road trip — the brain forms strong associative links between the musical elements (melody, rhythm, harmony) and the emotional context. Hearing that song later reactivates the entire memory network, including the emotions, sensations, and even scents associated with the original experience. This is why a single chord progression or melody can instantly transport someone back to a specific moment in time. The brain's reward system, which releases dopamine, is also activated by music, creating a pleasurable response that reinforces these associations. This is why songs from our teenage years are often the most emotionally evocative — that period of life is characterized by intense emotions and new experiences, creating strong memory-song pairings.
